Utopia, Five Hundred Years Later: From Thomas More to Artificial Intelligence

The dream of a perfect world and the uncomfortable freedom of those who inhabit it

The great danger of utopias is not that they aspire to a better world, but that they intend to achieve it without taking into account the freedom of the men who must inhabit it.

In 1974, I submitted a final year project at Gaztelueta College entitled “A Systematic Study of Thomas More’s Utopia.” According to my edition, More’s work was 64 pages long; my study reached 164. As you can see, even then, the art of synthesis was quite challenging for me. I had dissected that imaginary island into its various aspects: society, economy, work, education, morality, religion, and politics. And I thought I had grasped its inner workings. Half a century later, I return to those typed pages, filled with handwritten corrections, and discover that the most interesting thing wasn’t what they answered, but what they asked.

Utopia , published in 1516, is not, in my opinion, a ready-to – implement program of government. It is rather a mirror that Thomas More held up to the England of his time. It reflected poverty, inequality, the lust for wealth, and the abuses of the powerful, including a monarchical power that the cruel Henry VIII would ultimately wield with such arbitrariness that it would lead More himself to the scaffold. But the mirror also reflected a disturbing image: a country admirable for its organization and, in certain respects, unappealing as a place to live.

In Utopia, there is no private property or money in daily life; people work six hours a day, share meals, care for the sick, and strive to ensure that no one goes hungry. Customs are monitored, movement is regulated, offenders are severely punished, and every citizen is expected to behave according to a near-perfect standard. Equality is enviable; freedom, considerably less so. In my thesis, I pointed out this contradiction, albeit with the optimism—or perhaps the recklessness—of someone who hasn’t yet witnessed too many times how societies that promise to make everyone happy end up.

There is something deliciously suspicious about More. He called Utopia a “no place,” but he also plays with the idea of ​​a “good place”; he had Raphael Hythloday speak, whose surname semantically evokes an expert in nonsense, and inserted himself into the dialogue only to maintain an ironic distance from what he heard. It is a game of humanists, yes, but a very serious one: should we admire that republic, distrust it, or do both simultaneously?

In 1974, I was intrigued by the supposed “good man” without whom the whole edifice would collapse. If no one steals, if almost no one lies, if no one accumulates more than necessary, and if everyone willingly accepts common decisions, managing a society should be relatively simple. But not all islands are Formosa. The real problem lies in finding their inhabitants. And, if they don’t exist, creating them. Therein lies the perilous slope of many utopias: first, the perfect world is designed; then it is discovered that many people don’t fit the desired profile… and are an obstacle . History, from Stalin to Pol Pot, has shown the monstrosities to which the goal of building a perfect society by eliminating those who don’t fit into it can lead.

It is unwise, however, to dismiss More as a direct precursor of modern totalitarianism. That would be an anachronism and, above all, a far too convenient interpretation. His book is ambiguous, satirical, and critical of his own time. More was able to take fidelity to his conscience to the extreme of giving his life for it, but we should not try to make a Renaissance man into one of our contemporaries. His greatness does not demand that we accept all the provisions of his imaginary island: the enslavement of the condemned, the surveillance of behavior, travel permits, limitations on privacy, or the public administration of profoundly personal decisions. Over the centuries, we have learned that even the best intentions, if they become unlimited power, can take on a rather sinister aspect. And today, such systems of control can be exercised not only communally, as in the past, but also from a distant and unknown apex of power thanks to technology.

In this respect, the 20th century inoculated us—though not all of us—with experiences of social engineering and with the literary warnings of Zamyatin, Huxley, Orwell, and Bradbury, among others , who cautioned us about the thin line separating utopias from dystopias. Zamyatin, in “We” (circa 1920), was the first: he imagined a One State in which people are numbers, live in glass houses so they can be monitored, and are governed by a schedule. His policy is that total and calculated happiness requires suppressing freedom, imagination, and love. Freedom is what makes a person imperfect and irrational, and that is why the State considers it a disease.

In *The Open Society and Its Enemies *, Karl Popper contrasted gradual, correctable reform with grand schemes that attempt to reorganize the entire society at once. I find this a crucial distinction: in a democracy, the mistakes of those in power can be addressed through institutions, public criticism, and elections; the mistakes of the self-proclaimed savior who has eliminated these checks and balances tend to be far more costly.

There’s a question I’ve recently revisited elsewhere: why is freedom sometimes so uncomfortable, even for those of us who defend it so vehemently? We’d like a world without wars, diseases, betrayals, or injustices; a world where we all loved each other dearly, no one deceived anyone, and even neighborhood meetings were peaceful. But at the same time, we want to preserve our right to think, to dissent, to make mistakes, and, sometimes, to do the opposite of what we’re advised. We demand a freedom with a guarantee of results. It’s a policy that no company has yet dared to offer.

Dostoevsky masterfully presented this contradiction in the legend of the Grand Inquisitor from The Brothers Karamazov . Christ offers humanity freedom; the Inquisitor reproaches him for imposing too heavy a burden and proposes replacing it with bread, security, and obedience. The temptation hasn’t aged. The inquisitor and the instruments change, but the offer remains: surrender a large part of your autonomy, and I’ll spare you the trouble of deciding and provide you with bread and circuses, or… hamburgers and football.

Freedom is certainly not the unlimited right to harm others. It requires justice, institutions, and accountability. It also requires a minimum of material security: those who live in hunger or fear may possess theoretical freedoms but lack the means to exercise them. This is precisely why More’s egalitarian impulse is so valuable. But creating the conditions for a free life is one thing, and deciding in advance how that life should be lived is quite another. The common good cannot become a pretext for suppressing personal well-being , nor can the individual be reduced to an interchangeable part in a perfectly oiled machine.

From a believer’s perspective, the issue takes on a deeper meaning. If God had intended us to be incapable of error, we might be exemplary automatons, but hardly creatures capable of loving freely. And here believers and non-believers can agree: obligatory love, however well administered, ceases to be love. That is why we must distrust any political paradise that requires eliminating the possibility of saying no. True inner transformation is not decreed by law nor achieved through an algorithm.

Contemporary utopia no longer needs a remote island. A data center suffices. In 1516, a society so well-ordered that it barely needed money was envisioned.
